uncited: This family replaces the global implicit coordinate-to-radiance mapping of standard NeRF with explicit, learnable 3D primitives (Gaussians, quadrics, or neural points) to improve rendering efficiency and geometric fidelity.
Unlike grid-based or pure MLP approaches, these methods represent the scene as a discrete set of elements, enabling differentiable rasterization or local neighborhood aggregation.

This approach is distinct from [Signed Distance Function (SDF) Representations](12495-signed-distance-function-sdf-representations.md) by avoiding signed distance field constraints, and from [Voxel and Sparse Grid Representations](13738-voxel-and-sparse-grid-representations.md) by using continuous or parametric primitives rather than discrete volumetric cells.
**Explicit Representation:** The scene is defined by a set of $N$ learnable primitives $\mathcal{P} = \{p_i\}_{i=1}^N$.
Each primitive $p_i$ carries geometric parameters (e.g., position, covariance, quadric coefficients) and appearance parameters (e.g., color, opacity, feature vectors).
**Differentiability:** The rendering process is differentiable with respect to the primitive parameters.
This allows gradients from the photometric loss to flow back to the primitive attributes, enabling end-to-end optimization via gradient descent.

**Local or Explicit Evaluation:** Unlike global NeRFs that query a single MLP for any coordinate, these methods evaluate appearance based on local context (neighborhood aggregation) or explicit projection (rasterization).

The set $\mathcal{N}$ contains primitives intersecting the ray or projected to the pixel, sorted by depth.
The shift from implicit to explicit representations in radiance fields began as a response to the computational bottlenecks of ray-marching dense MLPs.
Early work like [Point-NeRF](15538-point-nerf-representation.md) demonstrated that point clouds could approximate scene geometry more efficiently than grids.

Subsequent developments, such as [3D Gaussian Splatting](13657-differentiable-primitive-assembly.md) derivatives and quadric assemblies, leveraged differentiable rasterization to achieve real-time performance.
These methods are widely used in real-time rendering, SLAM, and scenes requiring high-frequency detail or complex topology.
